title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
§17, Exemplum II. This applies the infinite Lagrange-type interpolation formula from earlier in the paper. Consider g(z)=sin(zΦ)/z as a function of z. It is even, and g(0)=Φ. Its values are known at the symmetric nodes z=±(n+k), k=0,1,2,... Interpolating to z=0 gives the weight of node n+k: the product over all other nodes of (0−z_j)/(z_{n+k}−z_j). The ± pairs combine, so each weight is an infinite product of factors (n+j)^2/(m(m+2n))-type, exactly as printed.

Euler names the weights 𝔄,𝔅,ℭ,... and takes successive ratios. Each ratio is an infinite product that telescopes; he evaluates it by letting an infinite index i drop out. This gives 𝔅/𝔄=2n²/(n+1), ℭ/𝔅=(n+1)(2n+1)/(2n(n+2)), and so on. In general the k-th weight equals (2n)_k/k! · n/(n+k) · 𝔄.

Everything then reduces to 𝔄=∏_{k≥1}(n+k)^2/(k(2n+k)). He evaluates it with his old theorem (Wallis-type products as ratios of beta integrals) using a=n+1, b=1, c=n, d=1. This gives 𝔄=1/(n B(n+1,n)).

Result: Φ·∫_0^1 x^n(1−x)^{n−1}dx = Σ_{k≥0} (−1)^k ((2n)_k/k!) sin((n+k)Φ)/(n+k)^2. Note B(n+1,n)=Γ(n)Γ(n+1)/Γ(2n+1). For n=1 this recovers Φ/2 = sinΦ − ½ sin2Φ + ... of Example I. For n=½ it gives the series of §22.

Check: Σ(−1)^k(2n)_k/k! e^{i(n+k)Φ} = (2cos(Φ/2))^{−2n}, which is real for |Φ|<π. So the twice-differentiated sine series vanishes, and the series is cΦ. Evaluating c at Φ=0 gives ∫_0^1 t^{n−1}(1+t)^{−2n}dt = B(n,n)/2 = B(n+1,n). The formula is therefore correct for |Φ|<π.
errors: No convergence condition is stated. The terms behave like k^{2n−3}, so the sine series converges only for 0<n<3/2. For n≥3/2 it diverges and holds only in an Abel-summation sense. Validity also requires |Φ|<π, which is not stated on this page; the Scholion §16 discusses the boundary only for n=1.
The interchange of the infinite interpolation product with the limit (the 'i infinite' telescoping) is heuristic, though the final ratios are right.

Next page (§21): differentiating the result should give coefficients 2n/(n+1), 2n(2n+1)/(2(n+2)), ... The printed/transcribed n/(1(n+1)), n(n+1)/(1·2(n+2)) are inconsistent. For n=1 that version would sum to log(2cos Φ/2) rather than ½. This is either a misprint or a transcription issue; worth checking against the image of p.172.

ideas.what: Infinite Lagrange interpolation of an even entire function sin(zΦ)/z from samples at the symmetric shifted nodes ±(n+k), used to recover its value at 0 (the arc Φ)
ideas.modern_name: Cardinal/nonuniform sampling series for a band-limited function (Whittaker–Kotelnikov–Shannon type; nodes ±(n+k) are a shifted lattice)
ideas.usually_credited_to: E.T. Whittaker (1915), J.M. Whittaker, Kotelnikov, Shannon; Borel, de la Vallée Poussin for precursors
ideas.where_published: E555 itself (Opuscula analytica I, 1783); the Lagrange/infinite-product interpolation is set up earlier in the same paper

ideas.what: Evaluation of the infinite product ∏(n+k)^2/(k(2n+k)) via the ratio of integrals ∫x^{b−1}(1−x^d)^{(c−d)/d}dx
ideas.where_published: E122 'De productis ex infinitis factoribus ortis' (cited by Euler as 'iam dudum demonstravi')

ideas.modern_name: Fourier-type series with non-integer frequencies; double integral of the binomial expansion of (2cos Φ/2)^{−2n}
ideas.usually_credited_to: Expansions of cos^ν x with fractional ν are classical (Euler, Lagrange, Daviet de Foncenex era; standard tables)
ideas.where_published: E555; whether elsewhere in Euler is unsure

missed.claim: Euler's exemplum is a sampling/interpolation formula for the band-limited function sin(zΦ)/z on the non-uniform symmetric node set ±(n+k), k≥0. That set is a lattice with a gap of width 2n around the origin. The result holds exactly when Φ<π, i.e. within the bandwidth. Also, the threshold n<3/2 for ordinary convergence reflects the growth of the node-generating function ∏(1−z²/(n+k)²). This places Euler as an early user of non-uniform cardinal interpolation with a family parameter n, which is not usually mentioned in histories of the sampling theorem.
missed.quote: Si arcus a, b, c, d, etc. progressionem arithmeticam quamcunque constituant ... ex eorum sinibus longitudinem arcus Φ definire.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A historical precursor for sampling theory and the completeness of exponentials {e^{±i(n+k)x}}; a possible worked example for the Kadec/Levinson-type perturbed-lattice literature.

deep.surprise_reason: The formula is correct and elegant, and its derivation via infinite interpolation is a genuine sampling-theory precursor. However, the identity follows easily from known binomial cosine-power expansions, and E555 is a known paper.
transcription_corrections: Line after 𝔅/𝔄: the telescoped product reads approximately nn/(n+1)^2 · (i+1)(2+2n)/(1(i+2+2n)) (i infinite), giving 2nn/(n+1); the bracketed [?] is a reasonable reading.
ℭ/𝔅 line: the factors as printed are 1(1+2n)/(2(3+2n)) · (n+1)^2/(n+2)^2 · (i−1)(4+2n)/(1(i+2n))-type; final value (n+1)(2n+1)/(2n(n+2)) is correct.
Page header: printed as ')170(' and ')171(' with ornaments; the page image is a double spread rotated 90°.
